title: The Agent That Wouldn't Answer
summary: A coding AI agent, OpenHands, mysteriously stopped responding to user input despite a fully functioning interface and build pipeline.
content:
We spent two evenings trying to get an AI coding agent to answer a message. Not to write good code, not to solve a hard problem — just to reply. The interface loaded. The build pipeline worked. Every health check returned green. And then you typed something, hit enter, and nothing happened.

The Symptom

The tool was OpenHands, an open-source coding agent that runs in a container and gives you a chat window, a shell, and a file editor. The pitch is simple: you describe what you want, it works in a sandbox, you review the diff. We wanted it self-hosted, running against our own models, so nothing left the machine unless we chose to send it.

It installed cleanly. The web UI came up. The container built. And then the chat pane sat there, blank, while the logs filled with SQL queries and nothing else. Silence is the worst possible failure mode. A crash tells you where to look. Silence tells you nothing.

Layer One: Configuration Drift

The first two hours went into a configuration file the application had stopped reading. OpenHands moved from a config.toml model to a settings UI and environment variables in its current major version. We were editing the old file, saving it, restarting the container, and wondering why nothing changed. It was being ignored entirely.

Underneath that was a second, quieter problem: the model identifier. The agent needed to know which provider to route through, and the prefix on the model name is what tells it. openai/ points at one code path, ollama/ at another, ollama_chat/ at a third. Get the prefix wrong and the request either fails outright or goes somewhere that looks like it worked.

Layer Two: The Context Ceiling

This one was the real culprit, and it took the longest to find because nothing about it looks broken.

Agentic tools send an enormous amount of text on every single turn. A system prompt explaining the rules. Eighteen tool definitions, each with a full JSON schema. A skills index. The conversation so far. On a cold start, that is roughly ten thousand tokens before the model has read a single word from you.

The local model we were using had a default context window of four thousand. Everything past that got silently truncated. The model was not refusing to use its file editor — it genuinely could not see that it had one. When we asked it to create a file, it politely explained that it had no such tool. From its perspective, it was telling the truth.

Raising the context window to sixteen thousand tokens fixed more than any other single change.

Layer Three: Hardware, and the Laptop That Crashed

The machine had an integrated GPU — one of the newer Intel chips that shares system memory with the CPU. Ollama, the local model runner, detected it and then refused to use it, because integrated GPUs are disabled by default. A single environment variable overrode that. Performance roughly tripled overnight.

Then we got ambitious and tried a 14-billion-parameter model. It needs about twenty gigabytes of memory to load. The laptop had sixteen, shared with the desktop, the browser, and the agent container itself. It crashed. Twice. Not a graceful out-of-memory kill — a full lockup, hard power cycle required. The lesson is unglamorous: on shared-memory hardware, the model either fits or the machine dies.

Layer Four: Limits Nobody Documents

The next stop was hosted models, which should have been the easy path. It was not, because every free tier has a wall and none of them are where you would look for them.

One provider caps free usage at eight thousand tokens per minute. The agent sends seventeen thousand in a single request. The request is rejected before the model ever sees it, and the client retries with exponential backoff until it gives up — which presents to the user as a two-minute pause followed by a generic error.

A second provider caps free usage at fifty requests per day. One agent conversation is twenty to forty requests. That is one good session, and then you wait until tomorrow.

Layer Five: The Container Fight

By this point the agent was responding, but the sandbox it spawns for each conversation kept failing to start. Three separate causes, all producing the same error message.

First, SELinux was blocking the container from opening the socket it needs to create sibling containers. Second, the container's DNS resolver was pointing at an address that only works in one networking mode, and the sandbox used a different one. Third, the network namespace that provides outbound routing had gone stale and was missing its address-translation rules entirely.

None of these are OpenHands problems. They are all consequences of running rootless containers on a desktop Linux distribution with security policies enabled. Each one took an hour, and each one looked identical from the outside.

The Stack That Worked

What finally ran cleanly was a hosted model behind an API key. We tested both free and paid tiers and both worked — the free ones just hit their ceilings eventually. The one we would recommend is DeepSeek V4 Flash, which is cheap enough that the cost is not worth thinking about and fast enough that the agent feels responsive.

The numbers are worth recording. A full session — writing a page, running it, fixing it, taking a screenshot of the result — came to one and a half cents. Total input was 261,000 tokens across the conversation, of which 91 percent were cache hits. That last figure is why agentic tools are affordable at all: the enormous system prompt and tool definitions are identical on every turn, so the provider charges full price once and a fraction thereafter. Without prompt caching, the same session would have cost ten to fifteen times more.

What We'd Do Differently

  • Start with the model, not the infrastructure. We spent hours debugging container networking for an agent that could not read its own tool definitions. The model was the bottleneck the whole time.
  • Skip local inference unless you have a discrete GPU. A small model on an integrated chip works, but it is marginal for agentic work. A 14B model needs a machine built for it.
  • Pin your image tags. Floating on latest meant the software changed three times in one evening, and each version had slightly different behavior. That is a terrible variable to introduce while debugging.
  • Never use --rm. It deletes the container when it stops, which means every restart is a rebuild and every lost log is a lost clue.
  • Budget for a paid API. The free tiers are real, but they are sized for chat, not for agents. A few dollars of credit removes an entire category of failure.

Where It Goes From Here

The working setup currently lives on a laptop, which means it works when the laptop is open and stops when it closes. The next step is moving it onto a server so the same agent is reachable from any device, at any time, without a machine sitting awake at home to serve it.

That is a different problem — deployment, reverse proxying, and a container stack that was not designed to host a program that spawns its own containers. It will probably take another evening. But at least this time we know what silence means.

  This post was written with the help of an AI — the same class of tool it describes. Every failure above is real, including the two crashes. The configuration files, the debugging decisions, and the crashed laptop are ours.
